terms.term: «Я знаю, ты здесь. Я знаю, что ты боишься. Боишься нас. Боишься перемен. Я не знаю будущего. Я не могу рассказать тебе, каким оно будет. Но я могу показать тебе, как начать его менять. Я покажу мир без контроля и границ, мир, где возможно все»
terms.gloss: A close adaptation of Neo's closing speech in the 1999 film The Matrix, casting Durov's project as a challenge to control and boundaries.
terms.why_hard: Treating it as original narration misses a major cinematic allusion; the wording should echo each target language's established Matrix translation where possible.

proposed.en: “I know you're there. I know you're afraid. Afraid of us. Afraid of change. I don't know the future. I can't tell you what it will be like. But I can show you how to begin changing it. I will show you a world without control or boundaries, a world where anything is possible.”

proposed.ja: 「お前がそこにいることは分かっている。恐れていることも。われわれを、変化を恐れている。未来がどうなるかは分からない。だが、それを変え始める方法なら示せる。支配も境界もない、あらゆることが可能な世界を見せよう」

terms.gloss: 'Reinforced-concrete' firm conviction — Soviet-era slang for an unshakeable belief.
terms.why_hard: The concrete metaphor reads oddly literally; needs a natural strength idiom in each language, consistently.

proposed.en: had learned, hard as reinforced concrete,
proposed.ja: 鉄筋コンクリートのように固く心得ていた

terms.gloss: 'Everything has its price' — the expat's cynical creed.
terms.why_hard: Must stay a recurring creed-phrase, not paraphrased each time.

proposed.ja: すべてには値段がつく

terms.term: благородные устремления существуют, чтобы набить цену
terms.gloss: Noble aspirations exist only to inflate the asking price (in bargaining).
terms.why_hard: 'Набить цену' is market-stall idiom (to talk up the price); literal translation garbles the sarcasm.

proposed.en: noble aspirations exist to talk up the price
proposed.zh: 高尚的抱负不过是为了抬价
proposed.ja: 崇高な理想とは値段を吊り上げるためだけのもの

terms.gloss: 'The guys are just haggling' — expat's dismissive read of VK's behavior.
terms.why_hard: 'Парни' (the guys/lads) must match the book's broader rendering of the VK founders' casual in-group.

proposed.zh: 这些人不过是在讨价还价。
proposed.ja: 連中はただ値切っているだけだ

terms.gloss: Soft/plush toys — a gift category in the VK gift shop.
terms.why_hard: Trivial but part of a recurring gift taxonomy; must match other segments' category names.

terms.gloss: The commission percentage VK demands on sales — 10% demanded, doubled to 20% as an ultimatum.
terms.why_hard: Percent-vs-percentage-points and consistency of 'комиссия' (commission) throughout the negotiation arc.

proposed.ja: 10パーセント／20パーセントの手数料

terms.term: кнопка, которая в один клик позволяет приобрести подарок
terms.gloss: The one-click buy button VK offers the merchant inside its service.
terms.why_hard: 'В один клик' is the fixed web phrase 'in one click'; must match other e-commerce references in the book.

proposed.en: a one-click button to buy the gift
proposed.ja: ワンクリックでギフトを購入できるボタン

terms.gloss: Fidgeting/squirming in his chair — the expat's discomfort.
terms.why_hard: Minor, but body-language verbs recur in character sketches and should be kept natural, not literal.

proposed.ja: 椅子の上でそわそわと体を動かしながら

terms.gloss: Skeptical turn/shake of the head by the programmer, without stopping typing.
terms.why_hard: Ambiguous gesture (shake vs. look around); 'покрутил' implies dismissive rotation of the head.

terms.gloss: Suddenly bellowed — the baseball-cap figure's explosive outburst.
terms.why_hard: 'Заорал' is more violent than 'shouted'; register of the Durov outburst matters for the character portrait.

terms.term: сунул руки в карманы черных брюк
terms.gloss: Hands in pockets of black trousers — part of Durov's trademark all-black dress.
terms.why_hard: The black clothing is a recurring Durov signifier across segments; 'black trousers' must be kept, not generalized.

proposed.en: thrust his hands into the pockets of his black trousers
proposed.zh: 双手插进黑色长裤的口袋
proposed.ja: 黒いズボンのポケットに両手を突っ込んだ

terms.gloss: Slightly lopsided, leaning forward — Durov's odd gait.
terms.why_hard: 'Скособочившись' is colloquial and physical; a literal 'bent sideways' sounds clinical rather than wry.

proposed.ja: 少し体を斜めに前かがみになりながら

terms.gloss: 'This figure's eccentricity' — ironic epithet ('деятель', a mildly contemptuous 'operator/character').
terms.why_hard: 'Деятель' carries Soviet-era sarcastic connotation of a self-important operator; neutral 'person' loses the irony.

proposed.ja: この人物の風変わりな振る舞い

terms.gloss: Free indirect thought of the expat: 'we're all respectable people here' — his shock at the outburst.
terms.why_hard: Sarcastic interior monologue; must be kept as deadpan, not turned into a quoted line.

proposed.zh: 我们这儿可都是体面人
proposed.ja: ここにいるのは皆まともな大人のはずだ

terms.gloss: The foreigner (same expat) — shift of epithet signaling the narrative viewpoint.
terms.why_hard: Epithet switching (экспат/иностранец/менеджер) for the same person must be tracked so translation doesn't invent two characters.

terms.gloss: Yet another epithet for the expat, from his own professional self-image.
terms.why_hard: Must be recognized as the same character; 'manager' vs 'the expat' consistency question for the whole scene.

terms.term: разный процент с разных категорий товара
terms.gloss: Tiered commission by product category — the deal structure at stake.
terms.why_hard: Legal/commerce phrasing; 'процент' here means commission rate, not simple percentage, and recurs in the whole negotiation arc.

proposed.en: a different commission rate for each product category
proposed.zh: 不同商品类别适用不同抽成比例
proposed.ja: 商品カテゴリーごとに異なる手数料率

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the dominant Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as 'In Contact' or leave it transliterated inconsistently; the book uses it constantly and the name must be fixed early

terms.gloss: Afisha, a Moscow-based culture and lifestyle magazine (1999–2015) that was the voice of urban Russian hipsters
terms.why_hard: Without knowing the magazine's cultural weight, a translator might render it as a generic 'magazine' or miss the ironic citation tone

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject
terms.why_hard: Name must be consistent across the whole book; patronymic and diminutives may appear later

proposed.ja: パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: Nikolai Kononov, the author of this biography (Код Дурова)
terms.why_hard: He is referred to by surname only here; a translator unfamiliar with the book's authorship might not realize this is the author himself being referenced in the third person

terms.gloss: A Hero of Our Time, the 1840 Lermontov novel; here used as a high-literary label for a 'defining figure of the era'
terms.why_hard: Capitalization signals the allusion; a translator who treats it as a plain phrase loses the ironic literary echo

terms.gloss: 'Digital elite' — the small caste of tech entrepreneurs who rose to wealth and power
terms.why_hard: The scare quotes in Russian signal distance/irony; dropping them flattens the author's skeptical tone

terms.gloss: 'Hordes of mini-Durovs' — a hyperbolic image of future clone-entrepreneurs
terms.why_hard: полчища carries a slightly pejorative/military connotation (like 'hordes'); a neutral 'army' or 'legions' would soften the irony

proposed.ja: ミニ・ドゥーロフの群れ

terms.gloss: 'Think globally, act locally' — a well-known slogan, here repurposed for tech entrepreneurship
terms.why_hard: This is a recognized English-language slogan; a translator should use the established equivalent rather than a literal re-translation

proposed.ja: グローバルに考え、ローカルに動く

terms.gloss: 'Far-Reaching Conclusions' — capitalized for ironic emphasis, mocking grand generalizations
terms.why_hard: The capitalization is a stylistic device signalling sarcasm; a translator who lowercases it loses the author's distancing

terms.term: Как Все В Мире Будет Устроено
terms.gloss: 'How Everything in the World Will Be Arranged' — another capitalized ironic phrase mocking utopian futurology
terms.why_hard: Same capitalization-as-irony device as above; must be rendered with equivalent typographic or rhetorical marking in each target language

proposed.en: How Everything in the World Will Work

terms.gloss: 'Dragged into his nets' — a predatory/fishing metaphor for user acquisition
terms.why_hard: The verb затащил is colloquial and slightly aggressive ('dragged in'); a neutral 'attracted' would lose the implied manipulation

proposed.ja: 自らの網に引き込んだ

terms.gloss: 'Stirs the imagination' — a set phrase implying fascination mixed with unease
terms.why_hard: будоражить has a slightly agitating, unsettling nuance beyond simple 'inspire'; a flat 'captures the imagination' misses the ambivalence

terms.gloss: Gopniki — aggressive street toughs, typically from working-class housing estates, associated with tracksuits, squatting, and petty crime
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render as 'thugs' or 'hooligans' and lose the specific post-Soviet housing-estate connotation that is essential to the setting

terms.gloss: Sitsevaya Street — a street name in the Kamenskaya/Kupchino area of St Petersburg, used here as a nickname for a housing cluster
terms.why_hard: A translator might try to translate the meaning of the adjective ('calico') rather than keeping it as a proper name

terms.gloss: Kamyshovaya Street — a street name in the same district, used here as a nickname for a neighboring housing cluster
terms.why_hard: Same issue as Sitsevaya; 'kamysh' means reeds, and the translator must decide whether to transliterate or translate the street name

terms.gloss: Cities beyond the Arctic Circle — Soviet-era settlements like Norilsk or Vorkuta where construction was limited to hilltops due to permafrost
terms.why_hard: A translator might simply say 'Arctic cities' and miss the specific Soviet industrial-town connotation of isolation and brutal planning

terms.gloss: Hills or hillocks, specifically the low rounded hills characteristic of northern and Far Eastern Russian terrain
terms.why_hard: A translator might use 'mountains' or 'hills' generically; the word carries a specific geographical register tied to northern Russia and Siberia

terms.gloss: Mixed wild grasses and herbs — a botanical/geographical term for the diverse herbaceous vegetation of meadows
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might say 'weeds' or 'wildflowers'; the term is a specific Russian ecological concept implying rich, varied grassland

terms.gloss: Stylobate — the raised platform or base level of a building, here the ground-floor commercial podium common in modern Russian apartment blocks
terms.why_hard: An architectural term that most English readers won't recognize; a translator must decide whether to keep the technical term or paraphrase as 'podium' or 'base'

terms.gloss: Squandered or embezzled the money — colloquial for losing or stealing construction funds
terms.why_hard: The verb 'просадить' is informal and implies reckless loss; a neutral translation like 'the money was spent' would lose the connotation of corruption or waste

terms.gloss: Excavation pits — large open holes dug for building foundations, common on abandoned construction sites
terms.why_hard: Might be rendered simply as 'pits' or 'holes'; the word specifically means foundation excavation pits, evoking unfinished Soviet/post-Soviet construction

terms.gloss: Giant prefabricated apartment blocks — the standard Soviet panel housing (panelki) personified as towering giants looking down on workers
terms.why_hard: The personification and the specific reference to panel construction (panelki) must both survive; 'giants' alone loses the housing type, and 'apartment buildings' alone loses the literary effect

proposed.ja: パネル工法の巨大な集合住宅

terms.gloss: A new metro station, the last on the line — almost certainly the long-delayed stations of the St Petersburg Metro's Frunzensky radius (e.g., Volkovskaya or later stations), notorious for construction delays
terms.why_hard: A translator unaware of St Petersburg's metro history would miss the irony of 'expectations stretching on for years'; this is a pointed local reference, not a generic detail

proposed.en: a new station, the last on the line

terms.gloss: Peat — the area around St Petersburg was historically marshland where peat was harvested and transported, explaining the drained swamps mentioned earlier
terms.why_hard: A translator might not connect the peat road to the drained swamps and the overall landscape description, losing the coherence of the passage's geography

terms.gloss: Espionage-style stunts (infiltrating faculties to gather content or provoke interest)
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as literal spy stories rather than framing it as a metaphor for guerrilla marketing tactics

terms.gloss: Abbreviation for исторический факультет (History Faculty) at a Russian university
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might leave it untranslated or render it as a proper noun without clarifying it's a faculty abbreviation

terms.gloss: The average/typical student; a set phrase in Russian journalistic prose
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might over-literalize as 'statistically average student' instead of the natural equivalent

terms.gloss: Colloquial verb for browsing the internet (лазать = to crawl/climb, used informally for surfing online)
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use a formal register like 'accessed the internet' and lose the casual 2000s tone

terms.gloss: Catalyst — used metaphorically for an offline event that would drive people online
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might keep the chemistry metaphor too literally; it needs to read as a strategic concept

terms.gloss: The Kremlin clock (chimes) on the Spasskaya Tower, iconic symbol of New Year in Russia
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might just say 'the clock on the tower' without evoking the Kremlin chimes tradition; the reader needs to feel the New Year countdown

proposed.en: The Kremlin chimes on the tower
proposed.zh: 克里姆林宫塔楼上的钟声

terms.gloss: The ruby stars atop the Kremlin towers, Soviet symbols still in place in 2004
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might not convey that these are the famous Soviet-era red stars on Kremlin spires, or might miss the ironic tone of 'didn't bother to remove'

terms.gloss: Demiurge — used ironically/grandly to refer to Zuckerberg as the creator of his world (Facebook)
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use 'creator' and lose the mythological grandeur and slight irony of the Russian

terms.gloss: Internet nerd/geek — задрот is a derogatory slang term for an obsessive nerd, here used self-deprecatingly
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use a neutral word like 'user' or 'enthusiast' and lose the dismissive connotation that makes the transformation dramatic

terms.gloss: Hacked a server — informal borrowing from English, standard in Russian tech/internet slang of the 2000s
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might over-formalize or miss that this is casual register matching the era's hacker culture

proposed.ja: サーバーをハッキングした

terms.gloss: Downloaded/scraped files — выкачать literally means 'to pump out', colloquial for mass-downloading
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might say 'downloaded files' without conveying the bulk, somewhat illicit extraction implied

proposed.ja: ファイルを吸い出した

terms.gloss: To promote oneself / gain traction — colloquial term for self-promotion or building buzz
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use a formal business term like 'market himself' and lose the informal entrepreneurial energy

terms.gloss: Military metaphor: preparatory bombardment before an offensive; here the PR buildup before the contest finale.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'artillery preparation' is opaque; needs a punchy military image consistent with the book's war framing of Durov's stunts.

terms.gloss: 'Miss Audience Sympathies' — the viewer's-choice title awarded by student votes in Soviet/post-Soviet beauty contests.
terms.why_hard: A fixed contest formula; must be rendered as a recurring title, not paraphrased each time.

terms.gloss: Mark Zuckerberg, founder of Facebook, whose Facemash stunt Durov's contest echoes.
terms.why_hard: The allusion to Facemash (rating girls' photos) only lands if the name is the standard transliteration in each language.

terms.gloss: A deliberately provocative 'bomb' of a scandal, referring to Facemash.
terms.why_hard: Reader must connect to the earlier Facemash episode; the scandal-blast sense, not a literal device.

terms.gloss: Downscaling metaphor: if Zuckerberg's stunt was a bomb, this was a grenade that still exploded before the final.
terms.why_hard: The bomb/grenade scale contrast must be kept so the comparison reads as calibration, not separate images.

proposed.en: a grenade that still went off right before the final
proposed.zh: 一枚照样在决赛前爆炸的手榴弹
proposed.ja: それでも決勝前に炸裂した手榴弾

terms.gloss: Vote-stuffing from a single IP address.
terms.why_hard: 2000s forum culture: 'нагнать' is slang for artificially boosting; must read as fraud, not just 'got votes'.

proposed.en: someone pumped in votes from a single IP address
proposed.zh: 有人从同一个IP地址刷票
proposed.ja: 単一のIPアドレスから票を水増しした

terms.gloss: Durov maintained the pose of a neutral referee.
terms.why_hard: The referee framing recurs in Durov's self-presentation as 'ensuring fairness'; should use one consistent role-word.

proposed.en: Durov kept to the role of referee
proposed.zh: 杜罗夫坚守裁判的角色
proposed.ja: ドゥーロフは審判の役割を貫いた

terms.gloss: Claiming not to be on the judging panel.
terms.why_hard: Distinction between jury and arbiter is the whole point of his dodge; both must be distinct terms.

terms.gloss: Bureaucratic doublespeak: 'I merely ensure the fair expression of the people's will' — an election-commission cliché.
terms.why_hard: Sounds like official election rhetoric; keeping the officious tone signals Durov's irony.

proposed.en: merely ensuring the fair expression of the people's will
proposed.zh: 只是保证民意表达的公正性
proposed.ja: 民意の公正な表明を保障するだけ

terms.gloss: Fake/fraudulent votes.
terms.why_hard: Period forum slang; keep a compact coinage used consistently for ballot-stuffing across the book.

terms.gloss: Seven discussion threads sprang up on the student forum.
terms.why_hard: 'Тема' is a forum thread, not 'theme'; and the forum is the earlier-established student forum, needs the same name.

proposed.en: seven threads sprang up on the forum
proposed.zh: 论坛上冒出了七个帖子
proposed.ja: フォーラムにスレッドが七つ立った

terms.gloss: 'The architect' — Durov as designer of the site/contest, whom students suspected of rigging it.
terms.why_hard: Title-epithet for Durov; must match how the book elsewhere calls him creator/architect of the network.

terms.gloss: To draw hatred upon oneself; the students believed Durov engineered the fraud to make himself hated.
terms.why_hard: Inverted PR logic central to Durov's persona — any strong emotion, even hatred, is engagement.

proposed.ja: 自分への憎悪を呼び起こす

terms.gloss: 'What matters is that you stir people' — Durov's credo that any emotional engagement is good.
terms.why_hard: This is a recurring statement of his attention-economy philosophy; one formulation should be reused later in the book.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the social network Durov founded.
terms.why_hard: Needs a fixed rendering policy (transliterate vs. translate 'in contact') applied book-wide; Chinese/Japanese conventions differ.

terms.gloss: Membership of VKontakte passed ten million.
terms.why_hard: Milestone figure; keep numerals and 'users/members' consistent with network-statistics phrasing used elsewhere.

proposed.en: the count passed the ten-million mark
proposed.ja: 利用者が一千万人を突破した

terms.term: репрессировать группы, разжигающие ненависть к создателю сети
terms.gloss: Ban or punish groups inciting hatred toward the site's creator; 'creator of the network' is Durov's favored self-title.
terms.why_hard: 'Репрессировать' is deliberately Soviet-political vocabulary; 'creator of the network' must match his established epithet.

proposed.en: to repress groups fomenting hatred of the network's creator
proposed.zh: 镇压那些煽动对社交网络创始人仇恨的群组
proposed.ja: ネットワーク創設者への憎悪を煽るグループを弾圧する

terms.gloss: He cancelled the audience-vote (students' choice) category.
terms.why_hard: Must connect back to the 'Miss Audience Sympathies' title; 'nomination' here means contest category, not award nomination.

proposed.ja: 学生投票部門を取りやめた

terms.gloss: Elevated literary cliché (Griboyedov's 'Громокипящий кубок') — the audience seethed and roared.
terms.why_hard: A bookish allusion a Russian reader catches; must choose whether to keep the archaic grandeur or flatten it.

proposed.ja: 観衆は雷鳴のごとく沸き立った

terms.gloss: Ironic use of 'occupied': the front row was taken over by sponsors, the dean and cronies.
terms.why_hard: The military/political verb is deliberate irony; a neutral 'took' loses the mocking tone.

terms.gloss: Vyacheslav Mirilashvili-era associate — here Levon Perekopsky, Durov's close aide.
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration must be stable across the book; also the assistant role should stay implicit as in Russian.

terms.gloss: The dean and the dean's inner circle of hangers-on, court-style epithet.
terms.why_hard: 'Приближенные' evokes a tsar's court; renders the satirical view of university power — keep the courtly flavor.

terms.term: вынос цветов до фонограммы и конферанса кавээнщиков
terms.gloss: Every detail staged, from the flower procession to the recorded soundtrack and KVN comedians' emceeing.
terms.why_hard: KVN (КВН) is Soviet/Russian student comedy league — needs an analogue or brief gloss; 'фонограмма' implies lip-synced playback.

proposed.en: from the flower parade to the backing track and the KVN comedians' patter
proposed.zh: 从献花环节到伴奏音效再到KVN喜剧社的串场
proposed.ja: 花の入場から音源、KVNお笑いチームの司会まで

terms.gloss: They had rehearsed everything in advance.
terms.why_hard: Shows Durov directing the show yet sitting in the audience — the puppet-master motif; keep the theatrical vocabulary.

proposed.ja: すべてを綿密にリハーサルしていた

terms.gloss: Bolshaya Morskaya Street, a major street in central St Petersburg leading toward Palace Square
terms.why_hard: Translators might transliterate inconsistently (Bolshaya Morskaya vs. Big Sea Street) or omit the 'Bolshaya'

proposed.ja: ボルシャヤ・モルスカヤ通り

terms.gloss: Palace Square, the central square of St Petersburg in front of the Winter Palace
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent throughout the book; some might say 'Palace Square' vs 'Dvortsovaya Square'

terms.gloss: Slang for crashing at someone's place, staying over without formal invitation
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as 'registered' or 'signed up' from the literal meaning of вписаться

terms.gloss: The wind-tunnel effect created by St Petersburg's arched gateways (подворотни) channeling wind
terms.why_hard: A translator might miss that подворотни are the characteristic arched passageways through St Petersburg apartment blocks, not just 'alleys'

proposed.en: the wind-tunnel throats of the gateways
proposed.zh: 拱门通道如风洞般呼啸
proposed.ja: アーチ門の風の通り道

terms.gloss: Moraines of a glacier — comparing snowdrifts to glacial deposits crawling over the cobblestones
terms.why_hard: The simile is geologically precise; a translator who flattens it to 'like mountains' loses the author's image

terms.gloss: One of the Rostral Columns on Vasilyevsky Island, a St Petersburg landmark with a viewing platform
terms.why_hard: Translators might not know these are specific columns on the Strelka of Vasilyevsky Island, not generic columns; also the idea of sheltering inside/behind one is a local detail

terms.gloss: People wrapped up like 'cases' or 'sheaths' against the cold — a recurring image in this passage (also in [112])
terms.why_hard: The word футляр means a case/sheath; the image is of people bundled so tightly they look like objects in protective cases. Must be consistent with its reuse in [112]

proposed.ja: 鞘に収まったような人々

terms.term: Двери в трамвае стреляли, как красные матросы
terms.gloss: Tram doors slammed like Red sailors — an allusion to the revolutionary sailors of 1917 who fired their weapons
terms.why_hard: The joke layers a sound metaphor (doors banging = shooting) with a historical allusion to Bolshevik sailors; a literal translation loses the humor

proposed.en: The tram doors fired like Red sailors
proposed.zh: 电车门像红色水兵一样开火
proposed.ja: トラムのドアは赤軍水兵のように撃った

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the subject of the biography
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently throughout; some contexts use full name, others surname only

terms.gloss: Copper coins, small change — colloquial word for low-denomination coins
terms.why_hard: Not just 'coins' but specifically cheap copper/small change; connotes triviality

terms.gloss: Occupied (a desk) — used with deliberate military humor for a schoolboy claiming the front row
terms.why_hard: A translator might neutralize it to 'sat at' and lose the ironic register

terms.term: третья строчка снизу яснее не стала
terms.gloss: An aside meaning 'the third line from the bottom hasn't become any clearer' — a self-referential joke about the text itself or about something written on the blackboard
terms.why_hard: This is a meta-textual joke; a translator who treats it as a straightforward statement about a notebook line will miss the humor

proposed.en: the third line from the bottom was no clearer for it
proposed.zh: 倒数第三行依然看不明白
proposed.ja: 下から三行目は相変わらず不明瞭だった

terms.gloss: Scratched/scrawled on the board — нацарапано implies rough, careless writing, not neat writing
terms.why_hard: A translator might use 'written' and lose the connotation of rough, hasty scrawl

terms.gloss: Arched gateways passing through St Petersburg apartment blocks into courtyards, a defining feature of the city's architecture
terms.why_hard: No direct English equivalent; 'archway' or 'gateway' is approximate, and the word recurs in St Petersburg texts

terms.gloss: Tasya, a diminutive of Taisia, a girl who sat next to young Durov in school
terms.why_hard: Diminutive form must be handled consistently; some translators might expand to Taisia or leave as Tasya

terms.gloss: A school satchel/briefcase — the standard Soviet and post-Soviet school bag, a rigid rectangular case
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'briefcase' evokes a business context; 'schoolbag' is more accurate but less specific

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject
terms.why_hard: Must be consistently rendered across the whole book; English readers may know him only as 'the Russian Zuckerberg'

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, Durov's close friend and VK co-founder/vice-president
terms.why_hard: Surname is unusual; a careless transliteration might vary (Perekopski/Perekopsky/Perekopskiy)

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russia's largest social network, founded by Durov in 2006
terms.why_hard: Must decide once whether to use 'VKontakte', 'VK', or a localized equivalent throughout the book

terms.gloss: Cut loose / went wild / lived it up — colloquial for suddenly spending lavishly after being constrained
terms.why_hard: Literal 'tore off' is meaningless; the register is informal and implies a release of pent-up desire for luxury

terms.gloss: A phrase Durov used as a personal mantra/slogan, implying they reshaped the world through VK
terms.why_hard: The ellipsis suggests a longer or repeated phrase; translator must decide whether to render it as a motto or leave it as an incomplete utterance

terms.gloss: Mantra — used figuratively for Durov's repeated ideological credo
terms.why_hard: Not a literal mantra; the word carries a slightly ironic or reverential tone depending on context; must be consistent if it recurs

terms.gloss: Binary code — the idea that human life is being converted into digital data
terms.why_hard: Straightforward term, but part of Durov's philosophical register; should sound grand, not dryly technical

terms.gloss: Wikipedia, cited as an example of self-regulating online communities

terms.gloss: Peterhof, a suburb of St Petersburg where the physics faculty campus of SPbGU is located

terms.gloss: The economics faculty of St Petersburg State University (СПбГУ)

terms.gloss: The law faculty of SPbGU, referred to by its students

terms.gloss: History faculty (исторический факультет), common university abbreviation

terms.gloss: Petty politicking / political scheming — pejorative term for self-serving political maneuvering

terms.gloss: Student council (студенческий совет), a student self-governance body in Russian universities

terms.gloss: Trade union committee (профсоюзный комитет) at the faculty level, which controls event budgets

terms.gloss: A 'passionary stratum' — allusion to Lev Gumilyov's ethnological theory of пассионарность (passionarity), meaning a driven, energetic minority
terms.why_hard: Deeply culture-specific term from Gumilyov's pseudo-scientific theory; most English readers won't recognize it, but it signals a specific intellectual register

terms.gloss: Student committee (студенческий комитет), another student governance body, distinct from студсовет
terms.why_hard: Must be distinguished from студсовет if both appear; they are different bodies with different functions

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov's student website for course materials
terms.why_hard: Capitalization varies in Russian; must decide whether to keep the domain as-is or localize it

terms.gloss: oral examination/discussion session used in Russian universities
terms.why_hard: No exact English equivalent; 'colloquium' may mislead

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov's father, Valery Durov, a professor of classical philology

terms.gloss: nickname for the nook by the philology department named after Professor Durov

terms.gloss: Russian university sub-department/chair
terms.why_hard: Not 'cathedra'; should be rendered as an academic unit

terms.gloss: conservative faculty who opposed the site
terms.why_hard: 'Conservative' may sound political; here it means academically/technologically conservative

terms.gloss: patchwork compilation, unoriginal cutting and pasting

terms.gloss: ageism, prejudice against older people
terms.why_hard: Borrowed English word; decide whether to keep as loan or translate native term

terms.gloss: phrase from Durov: old people trapped inside their own mental constructs

terms.gloss: English phrase left in Russian; refers to crowdsourcing/web collaboration

terms.gloss: both fame and a livelihood
terms.why_hard: 'Bread' metaphor may not carry in target; choose idiomatic equivalent

terms.gloss: hydrocarbon company, i.e. oil-and-gas firm

terms.gloss: Gazprom, Russia's state-controlled gas giant

terms.gloss: Bertova, a female acquaintance of Durov; genitive 'Бертовой' appears later
terms.why_hard: Surname gender and transliteration; avoid treating as male or possessive of Bertov

terms.gloss: quoted location nickname 'the School,' likely a St Petersburg university spot
terms.why_hard: Quoted nickname; literal 'school' may lose the local reference

terms.gloss: The experimental school 'Klassy' (Classes) in St Petersburg, a progressive institution with a Renaissance-inspired ethos

terms.gloss: To build a reputation or life story for oneself; here used in scare quotes suggesting the process was being engineered for them by outsiders
terms.why_hard: The scare quotes signal irony — someone else was constructing their biography, not them; a flat rendering loses the layer of agency

terms.gloss: Professional-technical school (профессионально-техническое училище), a Soviet-era vocational school with low prestige connotations

terms.gloss: Smolensky Cemetery on Vasilyevsky Island in St Petersburg, one of the city's oldest cemeteries
terms.why_hard: A translator unfamiliar with St Petersburg geography might not realize this is a specific landmark that anchors the school's location

terms.gloss: Dissidents — used metaphorically to describe the school's students and parents as political outsiders resisting authority
terms.why_hard: The word carries heavy Soviet-era political weight; a translator must decide whether to keep the loaded metaphor or soften it

terms.gloss: The Horde — a self-referential or imposed collective name for the school community, evoking a nomadic, unruly mass

terms.gloss: Mednikov, likely the director or key figure of the Klassy school
terms.why_hard: A surname appearing without first name; consistency in rendering across the book is essential

terms.gloss: Sanitary-epidemiological station, a Soviet/post-Soviet public health inspection body used here as a tool to shut down the school

terms.gloss: Chernaya Rechka, a metro station and area in St Petersburg historically famous as the site of Pushkin's fatal duel

proposed.ja: チョールナヤ・レーチカ

terms.gloss: Renaissance men — the school's ideology framed its students as modern Renaissance individuals, a deliberate self-mythologization
terms.why_hard: The phrase is part of the school's self-branding; a translator must decide whether to translate literally or find an equivalent that carries the same aspirational weight

terms.gloss: Colloquial/derogatory term for students of a PTU (vocational school), implying low social status

terms.gloss: Rebels/insurgents — the students and teachers who arrived to find the school locked

terms.gloss: Servants of the people — an ironic/sarcastic reference to officials (firemen, sanitary inspectors) who enforce closures

terms.gloss: Griz, likely a nickname or surname of the school's director
terms.why_hard: Unusual name that may be a nickname; must be rendered consistently throughout the book

terms.gloss: No help could be expected from anywhere — a fixed expression expressing total isolation

terms.gloss: To tame — used of authorities attempting to domesticate the wild, independent school

terms.gloss: Firemen — colloquial form (standard would be 'пожарные'); here part of a list of officials who burst into classes

terms.gloss: On an October morning — possibly echoing revolutionary imagery (October Revolution) given the context of rebellion and lockout

terms.gloss: The 'Strange People'—an epithet for Durov's programming team, likely a recurring chapter motif.

terms.gloss: A tight-knit group or clique, slightly derogatory or ironic, often implying exclusivity.

terms.gloss: Nerds, geeks, or bookish students (from 'botany' students, implying studiousness).

terms.gloss: Paul Graham, programmer and essayist, influential in tech startup culture.

terms.gloss: Physics Olympiad (competitive academic contests for school students).

terms.gloss: Founded their own state (metaphor for an autonomous, isolated community).

terms.gloss: Nerds (loanword from English, used ironically/affectionately for the programmers).

terms.gloss: Orange juice vending machine (automatic juicer).

terms.gloss: C++ programming language.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the subject of the biography.

terms.gloss: Allusion to Dante's guide Virgil: Elnara as Durov's guide through media/business matters.
terms.why_hard: The Dante allusion is compressed into an adjective; translators may drop it or misread 'медийный' as 'media-savvy' generally.

proposed.zh: 他在媒体世界中的维吉尔
proposed.ja: メディア界のウィルギリウス

terms.gloss: Deadpan excuse: 'I get carsick', Durov's ironic refusal of the money-and-car scenario.
terms.why_hard: The laconic absurdity is the point; padding it with explanation flattens the humour.

proposed.en: 'I don't want a car — I get carsick.'
proposed.ja: 「車なんていらない——車に酔うんだ」

terms.gloss: Moderator of the forum section for the international-relations faculty of St Petersburg State University.
terms.why_hard: A forum role tied to a university faculty, easily garbled into a university staff position.

proposed.en: moderator of the international-relations faculty section
proposed.zh: 国际关系系版面的版主
proposed.ja: 国際関係学部板のモデレーター

terms.gloss: SPbGU forum moderator, later a VK co-founder and shareholder, quoted throughout the book.
terms.why_hard: A recurring named source whose surname transliteration must stay identical across all his quotations.

proposed.ja: アレクセイ・コブィリャンスキー

terms.gloss: A proposed name for the future social-network site, modelled on 'Friendster', considered before 'VKontakte'.
terms.why_hard: An English-named candidate brand; must stay in Latin script and not be translated or pluralised.

terms.term: «Я был недостаточно прозорлив, чтобы самому вложиться»
terms.gloss: Self-deprecating quip: 'I wasn't farsighted enough to invest my own money'.
terms.why_hard: 'Прозорлив' (farsighted, perspicacious) plus 'вложиться' (to chip in capital) is a money-meets-vision pun that flattens easily.

proposed.en: 'I wasn't farsighted enough to put in my own money.'
proposed.zh: “我当时看得不够远，没能自己投资入股。”
proposed.ja: 「自分の金を投じるほどの先見力はなかった」

terms.gloss: A new breed/type of entrepreneur, one who ranks social effect above money.
terms.why_hard: Kobylinsky's coinage characterising Durov; must be rendered as a coined category, not as generic praise.

proposed.en: an entrepreneur of a new type

terms.gloss: Pushed money to a secondary place, i.e. subordinated profit to other goals.
terms.why_hard: The 'second plan' idiom has exact English/Chinese/Japanese equivalents that a careless rendering paraphrases away.

terms.gloss: Social impact/effect on users, as opposed to financial return.
terms.why_hard: Should read as a value metric the entrepreneur optimises; 'social effect' in English is too literal.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the social network Durov built, known abroad as VK.
terms.why_hard: Book-wide decision: keep the Russian name, use VK, or both — must be uniform across every segment.

terms.gloss: Rumour that VKontakte was a project of the FSB, Russia's federal security service.
terms.why_hard: The FSB acronym needs expansion for readers who don't know it, without breaking the quoted speech.

proposed.en: a project of the FSB, the Russian security service
proposed.ja: FSB（ロシア連邦保安庁）のプロジェクト

terms.gloss: Philanthropy/charity — used ironically: people couldn't believe the site wasn't profit-driven.
terms.why_hard: The irony ('people didn't understand such charity') must survive; rendering it straight makes Kobylinsky sound earnest.

terms.gloss: The paradigm/requirements of a social network as a product category.
terms.why_hard: Grandiose 2000s tech-speak; must sound like period vocabulary, not like an academic paper.

proposed.ja: ソーシャルネットワークのパラダイム

terms.gloss: The SPbGU student forum Durov ran, the predecessor community of VKontakte.
terms.why_hard: A recurring URL-as-institution; the Latin domain must be preserved verbatim, never translated.

terms.gloss: Epithet for Durov as the architect/designer of the new site (and of the forum).
terms.why_hard: Recurring epithet; must stay metaphorical ('architect of the project') and not become a literal IT title.

terms.gloss: Forum members/users, colloquial Russian net-speak of the 2000s.
terms.why_hard: Period slang needing a colloquial register ('forum folks'), not the formal 'forum users'.

proposed.ja: フォーラムの住人たち

terms.gloss: Real-name policy: the key design principle distinguishing VKontakte from anonymous forums.
terms.why_hard: A product-design term and a recurring theme; must echo the later real-name/anonymous debates consistently.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the central subject of the biography and co-founder of VKontakte.
terms.why_hard: His surname and full-name form must remain consistent across the book and follow each target language’s established convention.

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, an early associate of Durov who later became a senior VKontakte executive.
terms.why_hard: The passage uses only his surname, while transliteration and when to supply his given name require a book-wide decision.

terms.gloss: The power to shape other people’s thinking and command intellectual influence.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering as power ‘over minds’ can sound sinister or supernatural rather than socially influential.

proposed.ja: 人々の思考を支配する力

terms.gloss: Showed off ostentatiously and tried to make himself look exceptional.
terms.why_hard: The colloquial verb is mocking and disapproving, stronger and less neutral than merely ‘stood out.’

proposed.ja: いつも格好をつけていた

terms.gloss: Was passionately determined to start a business of his own.
terms.why_hard: The Russian combines a ‘burning’ metaphor with an idiomatic reference to entrepreneurship, not simply opening an unspecified affair.

proposed.en: was burning to start his own business
proposed.zh: 一心想创办自己的事业
proposed.ja: 自分の事業を立ち上げたいという情熱に燃えていた

terms.gloss: A trusted adviser or right-hand man, evoking the Mafia counselor popularized by The Godfather.
terms.why_hard: Treating it as a formal job title misses its ironic Mafia-film connotations and Perekopsky’s subordinate status.

proposed.ja: コンシリエーレ（側近参謀）

terms.gloss: By exploiting an opportunity that yields a large return with little effort or cost.
terms.why_hard: It can mean ‘for free,’ ‘on the cheap,’ or ‘without working for it’; here it describes easy-money business logic rather than a literal giveaway.

proposed.en: Big money is made only from a free ride
proposed.zh: 赚大钱就得靠不费力的便宜机会
proposed.ja: 大金は、ただ乗りできるような機会からしか生まれない

terms.gloss: To use one’s brains a little rather than perform prolonged hard work.
terms.why_hard: The literal image of moving one’s head is nonsensical; the tone is breezy and deliberately minimizes intellectual effort.

terms.gloss: Cultivated influence and an air of mystery as if they were roles in a game.
terms.why_hard: The construction implies deliberate self-fashioning and affectation, not that Durov literally played a named game.

proposed.en: played at being influential and enigmatic
proposed.zh: 刻意营造影响力和神秘感
proposed.ja: 影響力と謎めいた雰囲気を演出していた

terms.gloss: A wry declaration that accumulating money is Perekopsky’s chosen hobby and objective.
terms.why_hard: Rendering it merely as ‘I make money’ loses the deadpan collector metaphor and characterization.

proposed.ja: 私は金をコレクションしている

terms.gloss: Native speakers employed as language teachers, a common selling point for private language courses.
terms.why_hard: The phrase means native speakers of the language, not ‘language carriers,’ and functions here as education-market terminology.

terms.gloss: A man employed in or enriched by the oil industry, here the father of Perekopsky’s girlfriend.
terms.why_hard: Russian usage can imply an oil-industry professional or businessman, not literally an oil-field laborer.

terms.gloss: The language courses gained publicity, customers, and commercial momentum.
terms.why_hard: The colloquial verb can mean promoted, popularized, or became successful; a literal ‘spun up’ is wrong.

terms.gloss: One of the acquaintances who was due to teach suddenly became unavailable or dropped out.
terms.why_hard: Слетел is elliptical slang whose precise cause is unstated; translating it as flying, being fired, or crashing invents detail.

proposed.en: one of his acquaintances dropped out
proposed.zh: 有个熟人临时来不了了
proposed.ja: 知人の一人が急に来られなくなった

terms.gloss: A St Petersburg bar or café called The Idiot, apparently named after Dostoevsky’s novel.
terms.why_hard: The venue’s official styling and the literary allusion should be verified rather than treating ‘idiot’ as a description of the acquaintance.

terms.gloss: Fashion-conscious young women associated with the glossy, status-driven ‘glamour’ culture of 2000s Russia.
terms.why_hard: Neither neutral ‘girls’ nor literal ‘glamorous ladies’ captures the mildly mocking period-specific social stereotype.

proposed.zh: 两个打扮入时的时髦女孩
proposed.ja: 派手に着飾った若い女性二人

terms.gloss: Students or junior trainees undertaking practical work placements at a company.
terms.why_hard: Depending on the legal firm’s arrangement, they may be interns, trainees, or placement students; the choice should match later staffing terminology.

terms.gloss: A recruitment assignment to fill several additional vacancies or roles.
terms.why_hard: Позиции is corporate recruitment jargon for job openings, while заказ means a client commission rather than an order for goods.

proposed.en: a commission to fill several more positions
proposed.zh: 又接到几个岗位的招聘委托
proposed.ja: さらに数件のポジションを埋める依頼

terms.gloss: Nikolai Rogozov, a senior VKontakte developer involved in building its platform and API.
terms.why_hard: His surname must be transliterated consistently, and his role cannot be inferred from this passage alone.

terms.gloss: The application programming interface intended to let external software interact with VKontakte.
terms.why_hard: Here it means more than a generic interface: it is central to VKontakte’s proposed developer platform.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the founder and chief driving force of VKontakte.
terms.why_hard: His name and implied executive role must remain consistent throughout the biography.

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, an early VKontakte executive and Durov associate.
terms.why_hard: The comparison depends on identifying him and his established characterization elsewhere in the book.

terms.gloss: A mocking epithet for Andreev as a grandiose, fiercely independent figure who acknowledges no authority.
terms.why_hard: The improvised Russian compound is ironic rather than literal and may echo a recurring characterization.

proposed.en: Andreev, the self-styled master of himself, the heavens, and the moon
proposed.zh: 那个自诩“自己、天空和月亮都归自己做主”的安德烈耶夫
proposed.ja: 「自分自身にも、空にも月にも君臨する」アンドレーエフ

terms.gloss: Andrei Andreev, a Russian internet entrepreneur invoked here as a contrasting leadership type.
terms.why_hard: The passage gives only his surname, while understanding the contrast requires identifying which Andreev is meant.

terms.gloss: Did not resist uncompromisingly or defend his own position to the bitter end.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering about death would overstate the idiom and miss its workplace meaning.

proposed.en: did not dig in his heels to the bitter end
proposed.ja: 最後まで意地を張って抵抗することはなかった

terms.gloss: VKontakte’s developer platform for third-party applications, including its API.
terms.why_hard: It does not mean the social network in general; capitalization and context point to a specific product initiative.

proposed.ja: 開発者プラットフォーム

terms.gloss: An anticipated burst of energetic, self-motivated creative activity among outside developers.
terms.why_hard: Пассионарность invokes Lev Gumilev’s theory of history and is used here half-seriously for internet-era activism.

proposed.en: the hoped-for explosion of entrepreneurial energy
proposed.zh: 预期中的开发者创新热潮
proposed.ja: 期待された開発者の情熱的な創造力の爆発

terms.gloss: Durov did not have enough capable people or engineering capacity to carry out the plan.
terms.why_hard: The Russian literally says he lacked hands, but the intended shortage is staffing and attention.

proposed.ja: ドゥーロフには人手が足りなかった

terms.gloss: Kuzya, the familiar nickname of a VKontakte technical team member mentioned elsewhere in the narrative.
terms.why_hard: It is a nickname rather than a surname, and the person’s identity and preferred rendering require cross-checking.

terms.gloss: The company’s simultaneous struggles and development efforts in other areas.
terms.why_hard: The sustained military metaphor should sound forceful without implying literal armed conflict.

terms.gloss: The rapid user-driven spread of VKontakte across countries and platforms through network effects.
terms.why_hard: Вирусный is established internet-marketing language, not a reference to malware or disease.

proposed.ja: フコンタクテの口コミによる爆発的普及

terms.gloss: The Russian social networking service founded by Pavel Durov, now commonly branded VK.
terms.why_hard: The period-appropriate 2008 name and typography should not be inconsistently replaced by the later VK brand.

terms.gloss: The US social networking company and VKontakte’s principal global comparator.
terms.why_hard: Its established localized form and corporate-versus-service sense should remain consistent.

terms.gloss: Facebook was pushing toward the milestone of 150 million users.
terms.why_hard: The phrase extends the passage’s military imagery by treating a user milestone as a strategic height under assault.

proposed.zh: 正向“1.5亿用户”这一高地发起冲锋
proposed.ja: 「ユーザー1億5000万人」という高地を攻略しつつあった

terms.gloss: A sign-in mechanism allowing the same VKontakte identity to authenticate users across different services and platforms.
terms.why_hard: Авторизация is often mistranslated as authorization when the practical function here is cross-platform login or authentication.

proposed.ja: クロスプラットフォーム認証

terms.gloss: Highly driven activists and organizers who use VKontakte to circulate information and mobilize people.
terms.why_hard: The Gumilev-derived label carries ironic intellectual and activist connotations that a literal cognate would lose.

proposed.zh: 充满行动力的活跃分子
proposed.ja: 情熱に突き動かされた活動家たち

terms.gloss: VKontakte’s event-organizing function, used to schedule gatherings and invite participants.
terms.why_hard: A literal ‘service that makes appointments’ would suggest a dating or calendar service rather than social-network events.

terms.gloss: 'Plucking another bunch/cluster of autographs' — collecting signatures on his petition, framed ironically as celebrity autographs
terms.why_hard: Conflates автографы (autographs) with petition signatures; the irony that signatures are harvested like grapes must survive

proposed.ja: また一房の「サイン」を集め終えると

terms.gloss: Maksim Petrenchuk, SPbU history student and antifascist activist collecting signatures in the Kacharava case
terms.why_hard: Recurring character; transliteration must be fixed once (Petrenchuk, not Petrenchuk/Petrenchouk)

terms.gloss: 'Something operetta-like' — theatrically cloak-and-dagger, comically spy-like
terms.why_hard: Not 'operatic'; it mocks the would-be spy's costume as stagey, like an operetta detective

proposed.ja: オペレッタめいた雰囲気

terms.gloss: A goatee (lit. 'Spanish-style' beard)
terms.why_hard: Means specifically a pointed goatee, not a mustache or full beard

terms.gloss: A hard attaché case/briefcase
terms.why_hard: Russified loanword; not a generic 'case' — it completes the clichéd spy silhouette

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov introducing himself by the diminutive 'Pasha'
terms.why_hard: The diminutive signals studied casualness from a 'star'; keep diminutive vs. formal name consistent book-wide

proposed.ja: パーシャ・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: 'Star' — Durov already treated as a celebrity by students
terms.why_hard: Easy to overtranslate as 'VIP'; the joke is that a student coder is a campus star

terms.gloss: 'Here, sign it' — blunt imperative thrusting the notebook at Durov
terms.why_hard: Register: cheeky familiarity toward a celebrity; a polite rendering loses the point

terms.gloss: Dashed off a quick scrawl with the pen
terms.why_hard: Implies a hasty, perfunctory signature, not careful signing

proposed.ja: さっとペンで署名した

terms.gloss: Took his leave, bowed out politely
terms.why_hard: Old-fashioned courtesy verb; should stay slightly formal/ironic, not 'left'

terms.gloss: 'Having put on a polite smile' — a mask-like, performed smile while watching him
terms.why_hard: The 'putting on' (как одежду) implies calculation; flattening it to 'smiling politely' loses Durov's detachment

proposed.en: having put on a polite smile
proposed.ja: 丁寧な笑みを浮かべたまま

terms.gloss: A fraud/scammer — Durov was verifying the petition wasn't a scam
terms.why_hard: Register between 'crook' and 'fraud'; keep consistent with other fraud vocabulary in the book

terms.gloss: A sincere anti-fascist — the antifa activist milieu Durov vouched for
terms.why_hard: 'Antifa' as a Russian 2000s youth subculture term, not the later Western political sense

proposed.zh: 真诚的反法西斯主义者
proposed.ja: 真摯な反ファシスト活動家

terms.gloss: The Kacharava case — the 2005 murder of SPbU student Timur Kacharava, an antifascist killed by neo-Nazis, which the petition concerned
terms.why_hard: Without context a reader can't tell it's a murder case driving the petition; may need a gloss or footnote strategy

terms.gloss: The university rectorate — SPbU's top administration under the rector
terms.why_hard: Not 'the rector'; it's the collective executive body, a Russian university institution

terms.gloss: The governor (of St Petersburg, then Valentina Matviyenko), wary of public outcry
terms.why_hard: Unnamed but identifiable; decide whether to name her or keep 'the governor' consistently

proposed.en: the governor, who feared the noise
proposed.zh: 担心闹出动静的市长（州长）

terms.gloss: The historians — students of the SPbU history faculty
terms.why_hard: Means the history-department community, not professional historians

terms.gloss: 'Pokémonia' — the history faculty's private web forum (~200 users), name punning on Pokémon
terms.why_hard: Proper noun with a Pokémon pun; decide transliterate vs. translate, and keep the joke visible

proposed.ja: フォーラム「ポケモニア」

terms.gloss: Hung out — 200 of them regularly congregated on the forum
terms.why_hard: Slang 'tusovat'sya' (hang out), not 'gathered'; keep the casual internet-era register

terms.gloss: Durov's SPbU student portal/forum site he was building to absorb the faculty communities
terms.why_hard: Real domain, recurring throughout the book; must be rendered identically everywhere, never translated

terms.gloss: 'A crazy fire-starter/spark' — a madman who ignites crowds, an agitator figure
terms.why_hard: Compound slang epithet for the role Durov cast Petrenchuk in; keep both 'madman' and 'igniter' components

terms.gloss: The student trade-union committee (profkom), one of the two student power bodies
terms.why_hard: Soviet-era institutional abbreviation; readers need expansion, and it pairs with студсовет

proposed.ja: 学生労組委員会（プロフコム）

terms.gloss: The student council (studsovet), the self-governance body paired against the profkom
terms.why_hard: Must be terminologically distinct from профком; careless versions merge both into 'student union'

proposed.ja: 学生会議（ストゥドソヴェト）

terms.gloss: 'Both branches of power' — mock-constitutional framing of profkom and studsoviet as rival authorities
terms.why_hard: Irony: national-government language applied to campus bodies; keep the mock-solemn joke

terms.gloss: 'High style' (lofty bookish style); he gave wild drunken speeches without caring for elevated register
terms.why_hard: Literary-critical term (высокий штиль); not 'mood' — it's about rhetorical register

proposed.en: with no regard for lofty style
proposed.zh: 全然不顾什么高雅文体
proposed.ja: 格調高い文体など意に介さず

terms.gloss: 'The means are justified by the end' — the Machiavellian/Jesuit maxim Durov applies
terms.why_hard: Stock formula ('цель оправдывает средства') with recognizable allusive weight; use the canonical English form

proposed.ja: 目的は手段を正当化する

terms.gloss: Yuri Milner, Russian internet investor (DST/Mail.ru Group) who bought a stake in Facebook and later VKontakte
terms.why_hard: A careless translator may miss that this is Yuri Milner specifically and that the book's larger narrative frames him as Durov's key investor

terms.gloss: Alisher Usmanov, Russian metals and telecoms oligarch who backed Milner's internet investments
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration and his political proximity to the Kremlin matter to the rumor the text reports

proposed.ja: アリシェル・ウスマノフ

terms.gloss: colloquial: managed other people's money, i.e. invested capital that wasn't his own
terms.why_hard: Literal 'turned/spun money' is meaningless; needs an equally casual, slightly shady-flavored idiom

proposed.en: wheeled and dealt with other people's money
proposed.ja: 他人の金を回していた

terms.gloss: content delivery channels — the pipelines through which media reaches audiences
terms.why_hard: Sounds like a technical CDN term but here means media distribution broadly; register should stay semi-jargon, not fully technical

terms.gloss: the information environment of the future — the media landscape being shaped
terms.why_hard: Translators may render as 'media of the future' losing the surveillance/control connotation the rumor implies

proposed.en: the information environment of the future

terms.gloss: Lev Leviev (likely Vyacheslav Leviev or the VK co-founder memoirist referenced in the book), a source for the meeting's details
terms.why_hard: Must be identified from the book's earlier pages; wrong name form would break cross-segment consistency

terms.gloss: the book's recurring epithet for Durov (from 'Tema'/Тёма, his nickname), used affectionately/ironically
terms.why_hard: A recurring epithet that must be rendered identically across the whole book; literal 'totem' is wrong — it's a nickname based on his name Artiom/Тёма

terms.gloss: his knack for impressing people — Durov's showman streak
terms.why_hard: Should echo the book's recurring characterization of Durov as a performer; 'produce an impression' is stilted

proposed.en: his gift for making an impression
proposed.zh: 给人留下深刻印象的本事

terms.gloss: ironic conceit: a rankings table of intellectual-karate duels, i.e. battles of wits
terms.why_hard: Comic metaphor mixing martial-arts and business-talk registers; must stay playful or the irony dies

proposed.zh: 智力空手道对决排行榜
proposed.ja: 知力空手の試合ランキング

terms.gloss: two skilled PR men / self-promoters
terms.why_hard: 'Пиарщик' is mildly derogatory in Russian; 'PR specialist' is too neutral, 'flack' too harsh

terms.gloss: probed/sized each other up
terms.why_hard: Recurring verb for negotiation scenes; needs a consistent bodily 'testing' idiom, not 'got to know'

terms.gloss: kept his cards close to his chest, revealed nothing
terms.why_hard: Card-game idiom exists in all three languages but phrasing must be idiomatic, not literal 'did not open cards'

proposed.en: kept his cards close to his chest
proposed.ja: カードを見せなかった

terms.gloss: crude colloquial: 'we've had our share of shit' with the load problems
terms.why_hard: Register decision: vulgar but conversational; sanitizing loses Durov's brash voice, over-cruding breaks business-biography tone (esp. Japanese)

proposed.en: we've waded through plenty of shit with the loads
proposed.zh: 在负载上吃了不少苦头
proposed.ja: 負荷でさんざん苦労した

terms.gloss: 2000s Russian internet slang: how do you promote/grow your site
terms.why_hard: Period slang from the 'promotion/раскрутка сайта' era; 'how do you spin up' is anachronistic, 'how do you market' too corporate

proposed.en: How are you building up your audience
proposed.ja: どうやって知名度を上げているのか

terms.gloss: 'Organically' — Durov's terse reply meaning word-of-mouth growth without paid promotion
terms.why_hard: Single-word reply whose curtness must be preserved; must match the rendering of organic-growth concept used book-wide

terms.gloss: iPods given out as student promos at VK's launch (early viral marketing)
terms.why_hard: Refers to a specific historical stunt; needs recognition that these were prize giveaways, not purchases of iPods

terms.gloss: 'The Net' (lit. small fishing net) — the student newspaper at Durov's university where VK ads ran
terms.why_hard: Name is a pun (a scoop/net for catching) and a real paper title; needs a consistent title-plus-gloss decision for the whole book

terms.gloss: word of the project will spread like an epidemic — viral growth imagery predating 'viral marketing' commonplace
terms.why_hard: Should foreshadow the book's recurring viral/epidemic framing of VK's growth; keep the disease image

proposed.en: word of it would spread like an epidemic
proposed.zh: 口碑会像流行病一样扩散
proposed.ja: うわさは感染症のように広まる

terms.gloss: Russian set phrase: grew at a geometric rate — i.e. explosively, not literally exponential
terms.why_hard: False friend: literal 'geometric progression' is not the English idiom; 'grew exponentially' is the natural equivalent

proposed.ja: 幾何級数的に成長し続けた

terms.gloss: The VKontakte social network founded by Durov
terms.why_hard: Guillemets and spelling must be fixed once; en uses 'VKontakte' or 'VK', zh/ja need a stable transliteration

terms.gloss: A startup run by enthusiasts rather than professionals
terms.why_hard: 'Энтузиаст' carries positive amateur-passion connotation that 'enthusiast' alone can miss

proposed.en: a startup run by passionate amateurs
proposed.zh: 一个靠热情驱动的创业团队
proposed.ja: 熱意ある素人集団のスタートアップ

terms.gloss: Knocked the giants off their pedestal in one fell swoop
terms.why_hard: Mixing 'махом' (in one sweep) with pedestal imagery; literal rendering sounds odd

proposed.en: had toppled the giants in one fell swoop
proposed.zh: 一举将巨头们拉下神坛
proposed.ja: 一気に巨擘を王座から引きずり下ろした

terms.gloss: The giants of the Runet (Russian-language internet)
terms.why_hard: 'Runet' is a culture-specific term needing explanation or an accepted equivalent per language

proposed.en: the giants of the Runet, the Russian-language internet
proposed.ja: ロシア語圏ネット「ルーネット」の巨人たち

terms.gloss: Pirated blockbuster films uploaded by users

terms.gloss: Vyacheslav (Slava) Mirilashvili and Lev Leviev, the two co-founders/investors of VKontakte alongside Durov

terms.gloss: Venture capitalist; the text uses this as a descriptor for Milner

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, subject of the biography, here called by surname only

terms.gloss: the real-name policy (requiring users to register with their actual names)

terms.gloss: the Russian Ministry of Education

terms.gloss: university rectors' offices / administration offices of higher education institutions

terms.gloss: A student moderator on the History Faculty forum, central figure of this chapter

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, subject of the biography

terms.gloss: Durov, referred to by an epithet meaning chief architect of the platform

terms.gloss: A weirdo or freak, borrowed English internet slang common in 2000s Russian

terms.gloss: Lev Leviev, another childhood friend of Durov and future VK co-founder

terms.gloss: The Mirilashvili family — a prominent Georgian-Jewish business family in St Petersburg
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent with how 'Слава' is handled; the family name links the two

terms.gloss: Steve Jobs — used as a benchmark for Durov's design sense
terms.why_hard: Straightforward reference but must be consistent with how Jobs is rendered elsewhere in the book

terms.gloss: Tufts University in Massachusetts — the .edu domain Slava used to register on early Facebook

terms.gloss: 'About life' — a colloquial Russian expression meaning casual conversation about how things are going

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte
